messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When the bomb went off at the civic center, Priya was three feet from the main podium, about to give the keynote speech at a community safety forum. She had been a city council member for four years by then, thirty years old, proud of her reputation for being calm under pressure. The blast came from a trash can near the rear exit, and what she remembered most was not the sound but the white light, the heat on the back of her neck, and the strange quiet that followed for half a second before people started screaming. She had been thrown forward onto the stage, her glasses knocked off, and when she tried to stand, her legs would not hold her. Someone’s blood was on her hands, she never learned whose. She crawled toward the side door, certain that another bomb was coming, certain that she would not make it out, and that certainty—the absolute knowledge that she was about to die in a room full of her own constituents—had not left her since.

In the weeks that followed, Priya returned to work, but something fundamental had shifted. She had come to believe that the world was not merely unpredictable but actively dangerous, that danger was hiding everywhere, waiting for the moment she let her guard down. She found herself watching people differently now. At council meetings, she scanned the audience row by row, noting who sat near exits, who kept their hands in their pockets, who looked at her too long. She was vigilant for dangerous people in a way she had never been before, and she had decided that this vigilance was not paranoia but necessity. She told herself that nobody else understood how close disaster always was, how easily it could happen again. She had to be on guard all the time. She had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next.

Her daily life became a series of calculations. She stopped going to unfamiliar parts of the city for site visits, claiming scheduling conflicts. She avoided the civic center entirely, asking her chief of staff to attend events there in her place. At restaurants, she always sat facing the door, and she identified escape routes before she ordered her food. She had developed a habit of checking her surroundings constantly—every new room, every hallway, every parking garage—and she could not stop. At night, she found it harder to feel safe. She kept the lights on in her apartment until she fell asleep, and she slept poorly, waking at small sounds, her heart already pounding. She had stopped dating altogether. The thought of being vulnerable with a stranger, of letting someone into her home, of not being able to watch the door, felt impossible.

The consequences accumulated slowly. Her staff noticed that she seemed distracted, that she canceled meetings in certain neighborhoods, that she was irritable in ways she had never been before. A local reporter wrote a piece questioning whether she had lost her connection to the district, noting that she had not held a town hall in months. Priya read the article and felt a familiar surge of fear and anger. They did not understand. They had not been there. She had to be careful. She had to survive.

What finally brought her to seek help was a council vote on a new public transit route. The route would pass through a part of the city she had never visited, and she realized she could not bring herself to ride the train there to see it for herself. She sat in her office, staring at the agenda, and understood that she was no longer doing her job. She was afraid of a train. She was afraid of a neighborhood she had never seen. She was afraid of the next moment, and the moment after that, and she could not live this way anymore. She wanted to feel safe again, but she was not sure she remembered what that felt like. She was not sure she believed it was possible.
